replication.target_description: Unresolved row correspondence among printed candidate RMET condition effects, ART predictors and/or interactions.

reported_success.quote: we found no support for any short-term ... causal effects of reading literary fiction on theory of mind.

notes: Identity verified from the supplied full primary replication article: matching title, all seven authors and DOI 10.1037/pspa0000064 on page 1; nine text pages include Methods, Results, Discussion and References. Header has provisional volume/issue/pagination (Vol. 111, No. 9, 000), unlike the final bibliographic issue, but title/authors/DOI identify the work. No PDF was supplied. Original source and unassigned fields were not examined; their schema entries are placeholders. No replication locator is supplied; the broad description permits all three condition comparisons, ART associations and interactions, including different printed d summaries. Candidate evidence (not assigned values): p. 6 literary versus popular condition: 25.99), F(1, 191) ⫽ 0.83, p ⫽ .363, d ⫽ 0.05.; ART predictor: F(1, 288) = 95.16, p < .001, b = 0.37; ART × condition F(1, 288) = 0.67, p = .412. Literary versus no-reading condition: for those who had read nothing (Madj. ⫽ 26.25), F(1, 53.6) ⫽ 0.08, ... p ⫽ .775, d ⫽ 0.01.; ART predictor F(1, 361) = 139.37, p < .001; interaction F(1, 361) = 4.06, p = .045, with conditional b = 0.37 (no reading) and b = 0.26 (literary). Comparison N candidates printed p. 4: popular 303; no reading 369. These are candidate model Ns only, not assigned analytic Ns. Page 6 footnote 3 explicitly identifies the conditional b values as unstandardized coefficients in a model with transformed ART/RMET. No conversion performed. Additional p. 5 nonfiction candidates: nonfiction (Madj. ⫽ 27.02), F(1, 167) ⫽ 0.08, p ⫽ .775, d ⫽ 0.07.; RMET, F(1, 266) ⫽ 44.22, p ⬍ .001, b ⫽ 0.19; comparison N = 300. Page 7 Table 3 gives pooled descriptive condition d values −.08, .04 and .10, distinct from adjusted model d values. Reported_success refers to the authors’ paper-level verdict on immediate reading effects, not to the significant lifetime ART association.
